result: POC16/WDR90 localizes precisely on the microtubule wall in the central core region of centrioles in both Chlamydomonas and human cells, as demonstrated by U-ExM nanoscale protein mapping showing average distances of 0 nm ± 8 (POC16) and 2 nm ± 12 (WDR90) from tubulin.
evaluation: Claims C2, C16, C17, and C19 are well-supported by U-ExM experimental data with quantitative distance measurements and imaging evidence (Figures 1D-F, 1J-L, 1M-N, 1P). The localization is confirmed in multiple species with appropriate controls (POB15) and statistical analysis.

result: POC16/WDR90 is an evolutionarily conserved microtubule-associated protein containing a DUF667 domain similar to FAP20 and WD40 repeats. The DUF667 domain from seven different species directly binds both microtubules and tubulin dimers in vitro.
evaluation: Claims C3, C21-C23, C28-C30, and C34 are strongly supported by sequence analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B), microtubule-pelleting assays (Figure 2C), tubulin-binding assays (Figure 2D), and electron microscopy (Figure 2E). The evolutionary conservation is demonstrated across seven species with consistent biochemical properties.

result: The N-terminal DUF667 domain of WDR90 (amino acids 1-225) is sufficient to decorate and stabilize cytoplasmic microtubules when overexpressed, while full-length WDR90 shows minimal microtubule binding, suggesting possible autoinhibition or regulation by interacting partners.
evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by cell imaging data (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-E) and cold shock experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B-D). However, C27 is speculative regarding the mechanism. The differential behavior between N-terminal fragment and full-length protein is clearly demonstrated, though the mechanistic interpretation requires further validation.

result: WDR90-N pre-complexed with microtubules can simultaneously bind free tubulin, creating tubulin-WDR90-N oligomers with an 8.5 nm periodical organization on microtubules, similar to the 8 nm periodicity of FAP20 at the inner junction of ciliary microtubule doublets.
evaluation: Claims C31 and C32 are supported by electron microscopy data (Figure 2E-G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3F-G) showing dual binding capacity and periodicity measurements. C33 provides appropriate comparative context from published structures. The structural similarity to FAP20 supports the proposed functional analogy.

result: WDR90 is recruited to procentrioles in early G2 phase during centriole elongation and reaches full incorporation by the end of G2, with timing similar to the inner scaffold protein POC5, while Centrin and HsSAS-6 are recruited earlier in S phase.
evaluation: Claims C35-C38 and C89 are well-supported by cell cycle synchronization experiments with FACS analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B) and fluorescence intensity quantification (Figure 3A-H). The temporal recruitment pattern is clearly demonstrated with appropriate cell cycle markers and statistical analysis across multiple time points.

result: WDR90 localizes to PCM1-dependent centriolar satellites in addition to centrioles, as demonstrated by loss of satellite localization upon PCM1 depletion while centriolar localization is maintained.
evaluation: Claims C39 and C40 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-H) showing colocalization with PCM1 and specific loss of satellite localization upon PCM1 depletion. The PCM1 dependency is clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls.

result: WDR90 depletion by siRNA results in asymmetric loss of WDR90 from centrioles, with preferential retention at the mother centriole and loss from the daughter centriole, suggesting stable incorporation and a structural role similar to POC5.
evaluation: Claims C41-C44 and C46 are supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C, E). C45 is speculative but reasonable given the asymmetric depletion pattern and comparison to POC5. The presence of four Centrin-positive dots indicates duplication is not impaired, supporting the interpretation of asymmetric depletion rather than duplication failure.

result: WDR90 depletion leads to reduced Centrin and POC5 localization at centrioles but does not affect HsSAS-6 (centriole duplication initiation) or CP110 (distal cap) recruitment. The phenotype is partially rescued by expression of siRNA-resistant GFP-WDR90.
evaluation: Claims C47-C55 are well-supported by fluorescence intensity measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-O) and rescue experiments (Figure 3I-L). The selective effect on inner scaffold components (Centrin, POC5) versus proximal (HsSAS-6) and distal (CP110) markers is clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistical analysis. The partial rescue validates the specificity of the phenotype.

result: WDR90-depleted centrioles exhibit a slight increase in length (502 nm ± 65 vs. 434 nm ± 58 in controls) and a slight decrease in diameter at the central core region, suggesting defects in centriole length regulation.
evaluation: Claims C56 and C57 are supported by U-ExM measurements (Figure 4C-D) with appropriate statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test, p<0.0001 for length; ANOVA for diameter). The length increase is statistically significant and consistent across replicates. The diameter change at the core is modest but statistically significant.

result: WDR90 depletion causes marked alteration in the localization of inner scaffold components (POC1B, FAM161A, POC5, Centrin) in daughter centrioles, with coverage reduced from ~60% to ~20% of the centriolar lumen, restricted to a proximal belt. Centrin is specifically affected in its inner core distribution.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are strongly supported by U-ExM imaging data (Figure 4E-G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-E) with quantitative length coverage measurements. The use of CEP164 to distinguish mother from daughter centrioles is appropriate. The specific effect on Centrin's core distribution while maintaining distal localization is clearly demonstrated.

result: WDR90 depletion results in centriolar microtubule wall breakage in 10% of cells (15 out of 150 centrioles), with breaks occurring mainly above the remaining belt of inner scaffold components, indicating loss of centriole integrity.
evaluation: Claims C61 and C62 are supported by U-ExM imaging data (Figure 5A-D, Videos 1-2) showing clear structural breaks. The quantification is appropriate (15/150 centrioles) and the spatial relationship to the remaining inner scaffold belt is documented. However, the sample size for broken centrioles is relatively small.

result: WDR90 depletion affects the cylindrical shape (roundness) of centrioles, with 95% of depleted centrioles in top view showing ovoid-shaped or opened structures, indicating loss of the canonical circular architecture.
evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by U-ExM imaging data (Figure 5E-F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) with high penetrance (95% affected). The top-view orientation is validated by CEP164 appendage marker (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A). The phenotype is striking and well-documented.

result: WDR90 depletion does not alter CEP135 or glutamylation (PolyE) distribution, while FOP1 distribution is slightly disturbed but still present, suggesting the structural phenotype is primarily due to loss of inner scaffold components rather than general centriolar protein mislocalization.
evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by U-ExM imaging data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-N) showing selective effects on different centriolar proteins. The controls are appropriate for distinguishing specific inner scaffold effects from general centriolar disruption. The slight FOP1 disturbance may be secondary to inner scaffold loss.

result: POC5 depletion leads to slight centriole elongation (485 nm ± 64 vs. 434 nm ± 45 in controls), 10% broken centrioles (4 out of 46), shorter procentrioles in metaphase, and over-elongation after mitosis, phenocopying aspects of WDR90 depletion.
evaluation: Claims C67-C70 are supported by U-ExM measurements (Figure 6C-D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B). The phenotypic similarity to WDR90 depletion supports the functional relationship. C69 is confirmed by citation to previous work (Azimzadeh et al., 2009), providing validation.

result: WDR90 localization is not affected by POC5 depletion, indicating that WDR90 is upstream of POC5 in the centriolar assembly pathway.
evaluation: Claims C71 and C72 are supported by U-ExM imaging data (Figure 6E-H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) showing maintained WDR90 localization upon POC5 depletion. The epistasis analysis is appropriate and the conclusion that WDR90 is upstream of POC5 is logically sound based on the unidirectional dependency.

result: Double depletion of WDR90 and POC5 leads to enhanced phenotypes including strong decrease in cell number, complete removal of the POC5 belt, further centriole elongation (490 nm ± 72 vs. 372 nm ± 56 in controls), and ~30% abnormal centrioles (70 out of 260), demonstrating synergistic effects.
evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are supported by cell counting data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J), U-ExM imaging (Figure 6I-J), and structural analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, C-D). The enhanced phenotype in double depletion supports the functional relationship between WDR90 and POC5. The quantification is appropriate with sufficient sample sizes.

result: WDR90 is crucial for maintaining inner core protein localization, microtubule wall integrity, and overall centriole roundness and stability. POC16/WDR90 family proteins constitute an evolutionarily conserved central core microtubule triplet component essential for centriole architecture integrity.
evaluation: Claims C77-C83 are summary conclusions well-supported by the collective experimental evidence from depletion studies, U-ExM imaging, and cross-species conservation data. The conclusions are appropriately drawn from multiple converging lines of evidence including localization, depletion phenotypes, and structural analysis.

result: Based on sequence and structural similarity to FAP20, POC16/WDR90 is proposed to localize at the inner junction between A and B microtubules of the centriolar triplet, with WD40 domains potentially located inside the B-microtubule. Another protein, possibly FAP20, may mediate the inner junction in the proximal region.
evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are speculative proposals based on sequence similarity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and structural modeling rather than direct experimental evidence. While the structural similarity to FAP20 is demonstrated and the hypothesis is reasonable, the precise localization at the inner junction and the role of WD40 domains require direct structural or functional validation. The restricted localization to the central core (C2, C16-C17, C19) is consistent with but does not prove the inner junction hypothesis.

result: FAM161A, like WDR90, is a microtubule-binding protein close to the inner microtubule wall, raising the possibility that both proteins compose the stem and link microtubule triplets to the inner scaffold.
evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by citations to previous work (Le Guennec et al., 2020; Zach et al., 2012), but C88 is speculative. While the similar properties of WDR90 and FAM161A are suggestive, direct evidence for their co-localization at the stem or functional interaction is not provided. This hypothesis requires experimental validation through co-depletion studies, interaction assays, or higher-resolution structural analysis.

result: WDR90 depletion does not impair centriole duplication or microtubule wall assembly (as evidenced by HsSAS-6 and CP110 presence) but leads to strong reduction of inner scaffold components at centrioles and centriole destabilization.
evaluation: Claims C90 and C91 are summary conclusions supported by the collective data from C50-C51 (HsSAS-6 and CP110 unaffected) and C47-C49, C58-C60 (inner scaffold reduction). The selective effect on inner scaffold versus other centriolar structures is clearly demonstrated and supports the proposed specific role of WDR90.

result: Delta- and Epsilon-tubulin mutants affect centriole integrity across model organisms. In human null mutants, centrioles lack microtubule triplets, can elongate with HsSAS-6 and CP110 but fail to recruit POC5 (similar to WDR90 depletion), suggesting WDR90 may not be recruited due to missing A-B microtubule inner junction.
evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are supported by citations to published work. However, C95 is speculative—the authors propose that WDR90 might not be recruited in Delta/Epsilon-tubulin null mutants, but this has not been experimentally tested. The similarity in phenotypes (POC5 recruitment failure) is suggestive but does not prove the proposed mechanism. Direct examination of WDR90 localization in these mutants is needed.

result: WDR90 and POC5 depletion both affect centriole length, suggesting these proteins have a role in centriole length regulation and an unexpected role for the inner scaffold structure in length control, possibly through the concomitant elongation and inner scaffold assembly in G2.
evaluation: Claims C96 and C97 are supported by length measurements from C56, C67, and C75. However, C98 and C99 are more speculative interpretations. While the length phenotypes are clear, the mechanism by which inner scaffold components regulate length is not directly demonstrated. The correlation between G2 recruitment timing and length regulation is suggestive but requires further mechanistic investigation.

result: Centrioles have a nine-fold arrangement of microtubule triplets with an inner protein scaffold, are divided into three regions (proximal, central core, distal), and contain region-specific features including the cartwheel (proximal), inner scaffold (central core covering ~70% of length), and distal appendages.
evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C15 provide established background knowledge supported by citations to previous literature and the authors' prior cryo-tomography work (Figure 1A-B). C12-C15 specifically reference the authors' previous structural characterization (Le Guennec et al., 2020). This background appropriately contextualizes the current study.

result: Defects in centriole assembly, size, structure, and number lead to abnormal mitosis or defective ciliogenesis and are associated with ciliopathies and cancer. Centriole amplification in cancer can result from fragmentation of defective, over-elongated centrioles.
evaluation: Claims C7 and C8 are background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to published literature (Gönczy, 2015; Nigg and Holland, 2018; Nigg and Raff, 2009; Marteil et al., 2018). This contextualizes the importance of understanding centriole structural integrity.

result: Inner scaffold components POC1B, FAM161A, POC5, and Centrin are shifted toward the centriole lumen (15-28 nm from tubulin) compared to the microtubule wall, as previously reported.
evaluation: Claim C20 is supported by U-ExM measurements (Figure 1O-P) and confirmed by citation to previous work (Le Guennec et al., 2020). This provides appropriate comparative context for the WDR90 localization on the microtubule wall (C19) and validates the U-ExM methodology.

result: POB15 localizes internally along the microtubule wall in Chlamydomonas centrioles with an average distance of 12 nm ± 7 from tubulin, consistent with previous immunogold-labeling.
evaluation: Claim C18 is supported by U-ExM data (Figure 1G-I, 1M-N) and validated by comparison to previous immunogold-labeling (Hamel et al., 2017). This serves as an appropriate positive control for the U-ExM methodology and POC16 localization experiments.
